Given the following data for a function $f(x):$

| **$x$** | $1.1$ | $1.3$ | $1.5$ | $1.7$ | $1.9$ | $2.1$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $12$ | $15$ | $21$ | $23$ | $24$ | $25$ |

$$

$$

Approximate ${f}^{′}(x)$ at the point $x=1.7$ using a central difference approximation.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the central difference approximation

$$
{f}^{′}(x)≈\frac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{2h}
$$

 
at the point $x=1.7.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=0.2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(1.7) & ≈\frac{f(1.7+0.2)-f(1.7-0.2)}{2(0.2)} \\  & =\frac{f(1.9)-f(1.5)}{2(0.2)} \\  & =\frac{24-21}{0.4} \\  & =\frac{3}{0.4} \\  & =7.5.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Sam wanted to estimate the rate of weight growth of his new puppy. He took note of its weight every week, for $7$ weeks. The results are shown in the table below, where $W(t)$ is the puppy's weight (measured in pounds) after $t$ weeks from birth.

| **$t$** | $8$ | $9$ | $10$ | $11$ | $12$ | $13$ | $14$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $W(t)$ | $9$ | $10.1$ | $11.3$ | $12.4$ | $13.5$ | $14.6$ | $15.8$ |

$$

$$

Approximate the puppy's rate of weight growth $12$ weeks after birth using a central difference approximation with step size $h=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
We use the central difference approximation

$$
{W}^{′}(t)≈\frac{W(t+h)-W(t-h)}{2h},
$$

 
at the time $t=12$ and step size $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{′}(0.2) & ≈\frac{W(12+1)-W(12-1)}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{W(13)-W(11)}{2} \\  & =\frac{14.6-12.4}{2} \\  & =\frac{2.2}{2} \\  & =1.1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the rate of weight growth at the instant of time $t=12$ is $1.1\,\text{lb}/\text{week}.$

canonical_examples.problem:
A function $f(x)$ has values according to the table below:

| **$x$** | $0$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.3$ | $0.4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $1$ | $1.1$ | $1.3$ | $1.7$ | $2.5$ |

Approximate $f'(x)$ at the point $x=0.2$ using a central difference approximation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the central difference approximation

$$
f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x+h) - f(x-h)}{2h}
$$

 
at the point $x=0.2.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=0.1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(0.2) & ≈\frac{f(0.2+0.1)-f(0.2-0.1)}{2(0.1)} \\  & =\frac{f(0.3)-f(0.1)}{2(0.1)} \\  & =\frac{1.7-1.1}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{0.6}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{6}{2} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
A car engine is being heated from a temperature of about $-10^{\circ}.$ The temperature of the engine after $t$ minutes is given by $T(t).$  The graph of $T(t)$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14194746/assets/fe78a78911e2df9cdb488ec57b0e0a34bb56e18b57303d895dc8013b64a4afc3.png)

Approximate the rate at which the temperature of the engine increases when $t = 3$ using a central difference approximation with step size $h=1.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the central difference approximation

$$
T'(t) \approx \dfrac{T(t+h) - T(t-h)}{2h},
$$

 

at the time $t=3$ with step size $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(3) & ≈\frac{T(3+1)-T(3-1)}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{T(4)-T(2)}{2} \\  & =\frac{60-30}{2} \\  & =\frac{30}{2} \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of temperature increase is approximately $15^{\circ}$ per minute.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We've learned two methods for approximating the value of the derivative at a point by computing the rate of change between two points a distance of $h$ apart, where $h$ is small.

- The forward difference approximation computes the rate of change between the point $x$ and the point $x+h,$ which is a step of $h$ units forward.

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)- f(x)}{h}
$$

- The backward difference approximation computes the rate of change between the point $x$ and the point $x-h,$ which is a step of $h$ units backward.

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x)- f(x-h)}{h}
$$

Now, we will introduce the **central difference approximation**, also known as the **symmetric difference approximation**. In this approximation, we compute the rate of change between the points $x-h$ and $x+h,$ a distance of $2h$ apart.

$$
f'(x)  \approx \dfrac{f(x+h)- f(x-h)}{2h}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14194746/assets/48414a74d6f06fdec0f9b07c2a14f42c3a528b578b3a5f7a61cb4eff93016ac2.png)

Usually, the central difference approximation is a better approximation for $f '(x)$ than the forward difference approximation and the backward difference approximation. This is because for the central difference approximation, $x$ is the midpoint between the two points $x-h$ and $x+h$ that are used in the approximation.
